opus-5.5.text:
For me, the first thing is curiosity, real curiosity. Not the kind where someone has learned that research is a respectable career path and wants to publish papers, but the kind where they can't stop thinking about a problem. When I talk to a candidate, I usually ask them about something they worked on, and then I keep pushing: why did you do it this way, what didn't work, what surprised you? People who are truly curious light up at those questions. They'll tell you about the failed experiments in more detail than the successful ones, because that's where the interesting stuff is.

The second thing is what I'd call taste. It's hard to define, but in research, especially in a field moving as fast as AI, there are a thousand things you could work on and most of them don't matter. Taste is the ability to sense which problems are important, which directions are going to be fundamental versus which ones are incremental or just following a trend. You can't fully teach it, but you can see early signs of it: does this person ask "why does this matter" before they ask "how do I get a better number"?

Third, I care a lot about independence, but paired with openness. I want people who can drive a project themselves and don't need to be told every step, but who also aren't so attached to their own ideas that they can't change direction when the evidence says they're wrong. Good research involves being stubborn about the vision and flexible about the path.

And honestly, character matters more than people think. Research and entrepreneurship are both long, lonely, often frustrating processes. Most of the time things don't work. So I look for resilience, people who can sit with failure for months and still come in the next day excited. I also look for generosity, people who share credit, help others, and make the team better. A brilliant person who poisons the environment costs you more than they give.

Last, I don't put much weight on credentials. Some of the best people I've worked with didn't come from the most famous schools or have the longest publication lists. What I'm really trying to figure out is: in five years, will this person be someone who changes how we think about a problem? That's much more about the way they think than about what's on their CV.

r001.rationale: The response describes candidates who are genuinely curious and “can't stop thinking about a problem,” communicating sustained, self-driven engagement beyond assigned tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I look for is taste. That sounds vague, but I mean something quite specific: can this person look at a messy space of possible problems and pick out the one that actually matters? A lot of very smart students can execute beautifully once you hand them a well-defined task. Far fewer can tell you which task is worth doing in the first place. In research, and even more so in a startup, nobody hands you the problem. You have to find it yourself, and you have to be willing to say "this direction everyone is excited about is actually a dead end" or "this boring-looking thing is going to be important in two years." That judgment is hard to teach, so I pay a lot of attention to it.

The second thing is a kind of stubborn curiosity. I want people who genuinely cannot let a question go. When something doesn't work, do they just move on to the next idea, or do they sit there and ask why? A lot of the work I've been part of, including things like ConvNeXt or the work on representation learning for generative models, came from someone refusing to accept the conventional explanation and digging until the picture became clearer. That kind of persistence is different from just working long hours. It's about caring whether the answer is actually true.

Third, I look for people who are honest with themselves and with others. Research is full of ways to fool yourself. You get a good number, you want it to be real, and you stop looking for the bug. The people I trust most are the ones who, when they get a surprisingly good result, get suspicious instead of excited. In a company setting, this translates into people who will tell you bad news early. That's enormously valuable.

And then there's something harder to describe, which is whether the person has their own voice. I don't want to recruit a copy of myself. The best collaborators I've had disagree with me, sometimes quite strongly, and they usually turn out to be right about half the time. If everyone in the room agrees with me, we're going to miss things. So I actively look for people whose intuitions come from a different place than mine, maybe a different background, a different training, a different way of thinking about what a model is doing.

For entrepreneurship specifically, I'd add one more: comfort with ambiguity and speed. In academia you can afford to be slow and careful about a single idea. In a startup, you have to make decisions with incomplete information and be willing to be wrong quickly. Not everyone who is a great researcher enjoys that, and that's fine. But the people who thrive in both environments tend to be the ones who can switch between deep thinking and fast execution without getting paralyzed.

If I had to summarize it, I'd say: taste, curiosity, honesty, and independence. Technical skill matters, of course, but that's usually the easier part to assess, and often the easier part to learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes persistent, self-driven curiosity about unresolved questions, but does not say that this engagement extends beyond formal work time.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing I look for is curiosity. Does this person actually want to understand why something works, or why it doesn’t work? When a result is surprising, do they want to dig into it? In research, you spend a lot of time dealing with things that don’t work, so that curiosity has to sustain you.

I also really value independent thinking. You should be able to question an assumption, including my assumptions, and explain your reasoning. You don’t need to have the answer immediately, but you should have your own perspective and be willing to change it when the evidence changes.

For entrepreneurship, I’d add a strong sense of ownership. There’s always something missing—resources, information, a clear definition of the problem. Can you still figure out the next step and move things forward? That matters in research too. And across both, I want people who are generous collaborators, who care about solving the problem together.

r001.rationale: The response describes curiosity that sustains someone through research setbacks, but does not say they engage with a research problem beyond formal work time.

sol-6.1.text:
I look for curiosity, initiative, and the ability to think independently. When someone encounters something they don’t understand, do they want to dig into it? Can they turn a vague question into something they can actually investigate, without waiting for someone to specify every step?

I also value judgment. Being technically strong is important, but you have to ask whether a problem is worth solving and what evidence would change your mind. In research, experiments often fail. In entrepreneurship, your assumptions can be wrong. You need persistence, but also the willingness to adjust.

And I care about how people work together. Can we disagree openly? Can you acknowledge a mistake and learn from someone else? I’m drawn to people who are ambitious about the work and honest about what they don’t know.

r001.rationale: The response values curiosity, initiative, digging into questions, and persistence, but does not say recruits should engage with a research problem beyond formal work time.
